# Faculty AI literacy in higher education systems: a systematic review and future-adaptive framework

Yuqi Wu [a](http://orcid.org/0009-0009-3838-9924)[,b](#faculty-ai-literacy-in-higher-education-systems-a-systematic-review-and-future-adaptive-framework) and Yangjie Huang[b](#faculty-ai-literacy-in-higher-education-systems-a-systematic-review-and-future-adaptive-framework)

PRISMA-based systematic review synthesized 27 empirical studies to construct a future-adaptive faculty AI literacy framework. By anchoring 39 indicators across six **KEYWORDS** Faculty AI literacy; Boyer’s dimensions within Boyer’s scholarship model, the study reframes AI literacy as a scholarship model; future- systemic pillar of digital academic professionalism. Moving beyond transient tool- adaptive framework; meta- centric skills, the framework prioritizes enduring meta-competencies, speciﬁcally competencies; digital algorithmic logic and critical reasoning, as the primary mechanisms to safeguard academic professionalism; digital agency and prevent algorithmic alienation. The ﬁndings advocate for a systematic review paradigm shift from perception-based to performance-based assessment, 

operationalized through the proposed Artiﬁcial Intelligence Literacy Scale for Faculty (AILSF). This study provides a testable, evidence-based model of adaptive 

professionalism, ensuring faculty leadership evolves alongside emerging autonomous systems while preserving human-centered academic integrity.

# 1. Introduction

Given the growing importance of LLM-supported decision-making in educational systems, higher education faculty members play a pivotal role in shaping academic culture and preparing students for an increasingly AI-integrated world (McGarr et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021). The rapid evolution of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI systems such as ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs), is fundamen- tally transforming teaching, research, and service in universities. While these technologies present unprece- dented opportunities for innovation, they also pose profound challenges concerning digital competence, ethics, and the sustainability of educational systems (Dwivedi et al., [2023;](#author-contributions) Kasneci et al., 2023), raising ques- tions about digital competence as well as the sustainability of educational systems in the face of technologi- cal disruption. Unlike previous AI literacy frameworks that focused narrowly on speciﬁc tools, this study emphasizes that AI technologies are evolving beyond current LLMs. Accordingly, we propose a framework centered on foundational competencies and adaptive capabilities rather than tool-speciﬁc skills, ensuring its long-term relevance amid continual technological change.

The public release of ChatGPT in November 2022 marked a turning point in the digital transformation of higher education (Kasneci et al., 2023). LLMs are reshaping how faculty design curricula, conduct research, provide personalized feedback, and create interactive learning experiences. Unlike earlier educational tech- nologies, these systems o er conversational and generative capacities that support real-time instruction, automated content production, and adaptive learning. Such a ordances require that faculty develop soph- isticated competencies beyond basic digital literacy, including critical evaluation, ethical reasoning, and ped- agogical innovation in AI-enhanced environments. As AI advances beyond current LLMs toward more complex paradigms, faculty must cultivate competencies that transcend particular technologies and are grounded in enduring principles of critical and ethical engagement.

Despite the accelerating integration of AI into universities, research on faculty AI competencies remains fragmented, underdeveloped, and often disconnected from the realities of academic work. Existing frame- works largely target K-12 educators or general populations, leading to a mismatch between theoretical

models and the speciﬁc demands of higher education faculty in AI-augmented contexts. Previous research on faculty AI literacy has faced three major limitations: (a) deﬁnitional ambiguity, with over a dozen overlap- ping terms used interchangeably to describe AI-related skills; (b) contextual misalignment, where frame- works designed for K-12 settings are inappropriately extended to higher education; and (c) empirical fragmentation, with isolated studies lacking systematic synthesis to guide institutional policy and practice. This conceptual and empirical insu ciency leaves universities without clear guidance for assessing, develop- ing, or supporting faculty AI literacy at scale.

AI systems are also transforming the three pillars of faculty work – teaching, research, and service (Park, 1996) by altering how academics design curricula (Su & Zhong, 2022), conduct research (Kim, 2024), engage in scholarly communication (Tzanova, 2025), and uphold academic integrity (Currie, [2023)](#author-contributions). Unlike K-12 educators, university faculty navigate a unique professional environment historically deﬁned by Boyer’s model of scholarship ([1990)](#author-contributions), encompassing discovery, integration, application, and teaching. In the AI era, these academic roles are undergoing a fundamental transformation: (a) the scholar- ship of discovery now leverages AI to generate research hypotheses and synthesize complex data; (b) the scholarship of teaching involves mentoring graduate students and designing AI-enhanced curricula for advanced learners; (c) the scholarship of integration demands critical engagement in scholarly communi- cation and interdisciplinary knowledge synthesis; and (d) the scholarship of application requires faculty to lead institutional governance and model ethical AI use across professional domains. These interrelated spheres of academic identity demand not only technical proﬁciency, along with sophisticated meta- competencies such as critical judgment and disciplinary adaptability, dimensions seldom captured in the existing general AI literacy literature.

The distinct professional ecosystem of higher education further reveals the inadequacy of current AI lit- eracy conceptualizations. While K-12 teachers primarily use AI as classroom instructional tools, university faculty members engage with AI across the interconnected domains of knowledge creation, advanced peda- gogy, and institutional leadership. They must critically evaluate AI research methods, align AI tools with dis- ciplinary epistemologies, mentor emerging scholars in AI-enhanced contexts, and contribute to institutional AI governance. These tasks require an advanced level of AI uency that extends far beyond basic digital or technological proﬁciency.

Artiﬁcial intelligence was originally deﬁned as “the science and engineering of making intelligent machines” (McCarthy, 2007). More recent deﬁnitions have expanded this to include systems capable of per- forming cognitive tasks, including learning and problem-solving through innovations such as machine learn- ing, natural language processing, and neural networks (P. Wang, 2019; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019). In higher education, AI integration entails the thoughtful and systematic application of AI-powered tools and meth- odologies to enhance teaching, research, communication, and decision-making, while upholding ethical standards and human-centered approaches (Lachheb et al., 2025). Thus, it is not the mere availability of AI tools but the cultivation of comprehensive AI literacy that enables faculty to critically evaluate, ethically apply, and e ectively integrate AI to enrich the academic experience.

Research on educational technology and pedagogy employs a wide array of overlapping terms – _AI lit-_ _eracy_ (Long & Magerko, 2020; Ng et al., 2021a), _digital literacy_ (Bawden, [2008;](#author-contributions) Gilster & Glister, 1997; Martin & Grudziecki, 2006), _digital competence_ (Ferrari, 2012; Ferrari & Punie, 2013), _ICT literacy_ (Irvin & Macklin, 2007; Panel, 2002), “ICT competence” (Galanouli et al., 2004; Stuart et al., 2009), _technological ped-_ _agogical content knowledge_ (Koehler & Mishra, 2009; Mishra & Koehler, 2006), and _twenty-ﬁrst-century skills_ (Trilling & Fadel, 2009; Van Laar et al., 2017). This terminological proliferation re ects the ﬁeld’s interdisciplin- ary nature but has created conceptual confusion and hindered the formation of coherent frameworks tai- lored to higher education faculty. These terms originate from distinct theoretical traditions: for instance, digital literacy emphasizes critical engagement with digital content (Pangrazio, 2016), whereas ICT compe- tence stresses practical technology integration (Suárez-Rodríguez et al., 2018). Despite their di erences, they converge on the need for educators to develop technological uency to navigate AI-enhanced learning environments (Xu, 2024). Therefore, this study treats these terms as conceptually related and instead focuses on their shared insights into what faculty must know, do, and value when engaging with AI in higher education. However, without addressing the unique demands of academic labor, including research leadership, authorship, governance, and cross-disciplinary collaboration, these frameworks remain insu - cient to capture what faculty AI literacy truly entails.

## _1.1. Purposes of the present study_

While previous studies on K-12 teachers have yielded valuable insights into technology adoption and in uencing factors (Ning, Zheng, et al., 2025), research speciﬁcally examining this topic in higher education faculty remains limited. Faculty members face distinct challenges in AI integration that di erentiate them from other educational professionals (Jensen, 2011), including (a) advanced research methodologies requir- ing sophisticated AI tools and analytical capabilities (Wang, Zhao, et al., 2025), (b) graduate-level pedagogy demanding complex AI applications (Alzahrani & Alzahrani, [2024)](#author-contributions), (c) scholarly publishing and peer review in AI-mediated environments (Lan et al., 2025), (d) interdisciplinary collaboration across academic domains (Chiu et al., [2024)](#author-contributions), and (e) service responsibilities involving AI policy and governance (Chan, [2023)](#author-contributions). To address these challenges, this review identiﬁes the deﬁning characteristics of faculty AI literacy and di eren- tiates it from frameworks designed for other populations.

Accordingly, this systematic review of empirical studies on faculty AI literacy pursues three objectives: (a) to deﬁne and conceptualize faculty AI literacy within higher education contexts; (b) to identify the charac- teristics of empirical research on this topic; and (c) to synthesize and conceptualize the key indicators and dimensions of faculty AI literacy across disciplines and institutional settings. These aims are guided by the following research questions: 

RQ1. How is faculty AI literacy deﬁned and conceptualized in the higher education literature?

RQ2. What are the characteristics of studies on faculty AI literacy (e.g. study location, institutional type, discipline, research design, sample, and ﬁndings)?

RQ3. What indicators and dimensions of faculty AI literacy emerge across academic contexts and institutional settings?

## _1.2. Theoretical positioning of the present study_

University faculty members’ professional responsibilities inherently involve creating, managing, and evalu- ating various forms of AI-enhanced data and technological resources for multiple complex purposes across the interconnected domains of teaching, research, and service. For example, faculty use AI technol- ogies to enhance research methodologies and data analysis (Crompton & Burke, [2023;](#author-contributions) Ekundayo et al., 2024; Perkins & Roe, 2024), to design and deliver innovative pedagogical approaches in undergraduate and graduate education (Pedro et al., 2019; Southworth et al., 2023), to streamline administrative and service responsibilities while maintaining academic standards (Ahmad et al., [2022;](#author-contributions) George & Wooden, 2023), to uphold academic integrity and ethical standards in AI-augmented environments (Currie, [2023;](#author-contributions) Mijwil et al., 2023), and to foster AI-informed scholarly communication and collaboration across disciplinary boundaries (Klein, 2021; Nicholas et al., 2025). Thus, faculty AI literacy signiﬁcantly impacts technology inte- gration practices across all dimensions of academic work (teaching, research, and service) while simul- taneously shaping institutional culture and student learning outcomes (Chan, [2023;](#author-contributions) Ghamrawi et al., 2024; Pedro et al., 2019; J. Zhang & Zhang, 2024).

As such, there appears to be broad acknowledgment of the importance of faculty AI literacy in both higher education research and institutional practice. However, the existing literature on AI literacy does not deﬁnitively clarify how faculty AI literacy di ers from that of educators in general, which serves as the critical inquiry of our systematic review. To tackle this question, we have adopted the theoretical framework proposed by Ng et al. (Ng et al., 2021b) in their comprehensive analysis of AI literacy conceptualizations. Their theoretical framework emphasizes the diverse _audiences_ or users of AI technologies and provides an overview of AI literacy deﬁnitions for various educational contexts. They identify two broad categories: the ﬁrst focuses on AI literacy for students, citizens, and any individuals who do not hold professional edu- cational roles (Long & Magerko, 2020; Touretzky et al., 2019), while the second centers on the AI literacy of educational professionals in general (Ng et al., 2021a; Ning, Zhang, et al., 2025).

In the ﬁrst category, general AI literacy is deﬁned as the ability to “critically evaluate AI technologies; com- municate and collaborate e ectively with AI; and use AI as a tool online, at home, and in the workplace” (Long & Magerko, 2020). For the second category, educational AI literacy is a multifaceted competency that encompasses four core dimensions described by Ng et al. (2021b): 

4 Y. WU AND Y. HUANG

1. _Know and Understand AI_: The ability to comprehend fundamental AI concepts, functions, and technol- ogies, even without prior technical knowledge. This includes understanding how AI works behind every- day applications and services.
2. _Apply AI_: The capability to use AI concepts and tools in various contexts and scenarios, integrating AI knowledge into problem-solving and creative tasks.
3. _Evaluate and Create AI_: Higher-order thinking skills such as evaluating, designing, predicting, or commu- nicating with AI technologies. This includes the ability to critically assess AI outputs and contribute to AI development or content creation.
4. _AI Ethics_: Awareness of ethical, social, and human-centered issues in AI, including fairness, accountability, transparency, and the societal impact of AI technologies.

While Ng et al.’s framework provides a broad foundation, our study extends it by emphasizing meta-com- petenciesthe adaptive, transferable capabilities that enable faculty to evaluate, integrate, and ethically apply emerging AI systems across shifting technological paradigms.

By articulating the unique features of faculty AI literacy, spanning research excellence, advanced peda- gogy, scholarly ethics, and interdisciplinary collaboration, this study bridges conceptual and practical gaps in existing research. A theoretically informed and sustainable deﬁnition of faculty AI literacy can guide institutional policy, faculty development programs, and professional evaluation systems, ensuring that higher education evolves alongside AI while preserving academic integrity and human-centered values. Unlike tool-speciﬁc frameworks, which rapidly become obsolete, our proposed framework prioritizes principle-based, enduring competencies that remain relevant as AI continues to advance.

# 2. Methods

We identiﬁed relevant studies using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al., 2010). PRISMA, a widely used framework for reporting and synthesizing literature reviews, involves four main procedures: (a) literature search, (b) initial screening of documents, 

1. full-text review, and (d) analysis of the ﬁnal set of documents. Figure 1 presents a summary of this pro- cedure, and a detailed description is presented below.

## _2.1. Literature search and data sources_

The ﬁrst step involved identifying relevant studies through comprehensive database searches. Our literature search was conducted using three major academic databases: Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and EBSCO. We extracted all empirical studies that appeared to examine faculty AI literacy or included relevant foci (e.g. faculty AI competency, AI integration in higher education, AI skill development for academics). The upper and lower boundaries for publication year were June 2025 and 2015, respectively. In our initial search, we used the following keywords and their combinations: university, faculty, professor, instructor, academic sta , higher education, college, artiﬁcial intelligence, AI, machine learning, AI literacy, AI competency, AI skills, AI integration, AI adoption, AI acceptance, technology literacy, digital competency, and professional development. Among them, the primary conceptual constructs of this review were AI literacy, AI compe- tency, and AI integration among college teachers. Table 1 presents the search strategy syntax used for each database. We identiﬁed 9,244 studies in this initial search across the three databases: Scopus (n = 6,148), Web of Science (n = 3,044), and EBSCO (n = 52).

## _2.2. Screening process_

The second step involved screening the selected studies based on pre-established inclusion and exclusion criteria. First, duplicates were systematically removed using Covidence software, which identiﬁed 1,360 duplicate records, resulting in 7,884 unique studies for screening. As shown in [Figure 2,](#23-full-text-review) the temporal distri- bution of the identiﬁed studies demonstrates the rapid emergence of faculty AI literacy research, with the majority of relevant publications appearing in the most recent years, re ecting the ﬁeld’s response to recent advances in generative AI technologies.

The inclusion criteria for our review studies were (a) topics directly related to the key constructs (faculty AI literacy, AI competency, or AI integration in higher education contexts), (b) higher edu- cation context (excluding studies focusing on K-12 education, vocational training, and corporate set- tings), (c) full text available in English, (d) empirical studies employing quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-methods approaches with systematic data collection and analysis, and (e) publications in peer-reviewed journal articles (excluding book chapters, conference papers, dissertations, and grey literature).

To enhance transparency, [Table 2](#23-full-text-review) presents the complete inclusion and exclusion criteria applied during the screening process. After applying these screening criteria, 7,815 articles were excluded, leaving 69 articles for full-text assessment.

Grey literature, including conference proceedings, dissertations, technical reports, and preprints, was intentionally excluded to prioritize empirical rigor and replicability, as these sources typically do not undergo the same level of peer review as journal articles. While this decision enhances the reliability of the synthesized indicators, we acknowledge that it may introduce publication bias, as studies with null or negative ﬁndings are more likely to appear in grey literature (see Section 4.7 for further discussion).

## _2.3. Full-text review_

In the third step, the full texts of the 69 journal articles were comprehensively reviewed to evaluate their eligibility using our inclusion criteria. Two authors independently evaluated all retrieved articles for align- ment with the review’s research objectives, scope, and methodological requirements.

This evaluation process resulted in the exclusion of 42 articles for the following reasons: 37 studies did not meet the predeﬁned inclusion criteria regarding the conceptualization and operationalization of faculty AI literacy, and 5 studies involved sample populations outside the scope of higher education faculty. After this full-text assessment, 27 articles were determined to satisfy all inclusion criteria and were therefore included in the ﬁnal synthesis (see Figure 1).

Regarding study quality assessment, given the substantial heterogeneity of included study designs (ranging from cross-sectional surveys and structural equation modeling to qualitative case studies, scoping reviews, and mixed-methods investigations), applying a single standardized quality appraisal tool (e.g. MMAT or CASP) was deemed inappropriate. Instead, we adopted a qualitative appraisal approach during the full-text review stage, evaluating each study against four methodological rigor indicators: (a) clearly deﬁned research questions or objectives, (b) systematic and transparent data collection procedures, 

1. appropriate analytical methods aligned with the research design, and (d) coherent reporting of ﬁndings with adequate evidence.

Studies that did not satisfy these inclusion criteria were excluded at the full-text review stage. While this approach ensured a consistent minimum standard of methodological rigor across diverse study types, the absence of a formal scoring protocol is acknowledged as a limitation of the review (see Section 4.7).

The signiﬁcant reduction from 9,244 initial records to 27 ﬁnal studies re ects the ﬁeld’s current conceptual immaturity. While _artiﬁcial intelligence_ is a ubiquitous keyword, a total of 5,156 excluded records did not meet the inclusion criteria regarding the explicit conceptualization and operationalization of AI literacy as a measurable, role-dependent construct. By prioritizing peer-reviewed empirical evidence over anecdotal accounts and non-systematic descriptions of emerging technologies, this review ensures that the identiﬁed indicators possess high empirical reliability.

## _2.4. Analytic approach_

We conducted a systematic thematic analysis of the ﬁnal selection of 27 studies to identify and synthesize components of faculty AI literacy in higher education. Our analytic procedure followed the thematic syn- thesis approach outlined by Thomas and Harden (2008), comprising three sequential phases: (a) line-by- line coding of relevant text segments, (b) grouping and categorizing speciﬁc codes, and (c) developing over- arching themes by clustering conceptually related codes.

Two researchers independently coded all 27 articles, focusing on text segments that described faculty AI competencies, skills, knowledge areas, attitudes, or behavioral indicators. This process included both explicitly stated competencies and implicit indicators inferred from study ﬁndings. To ensure methodo- logical rigor, inter-rater reliability was assessed after independent coding. Substantial agreement was achieved, with Cohen’s κ = 0.79 for primary code categories and κ = 0.73 for sub-codes, both exceeding the commonly accepted threshold of 0.70 for qualitative thematic analysis (Landis & Koch, 1977). Approximately 18% of coding discrepancies were resolved through structured consensus discussions, and a third researcher adjudicated any remaining disagreements, resulting in full agreement on the ﬁnal coding framework.

Themes were developed following a bottom-up, inductive logic, whereby related codes were iteratively grouped into broader thematic categories. During this process, we di erentiated between indicators (speciﬁc, observable elements of faculty AI literacy) and conceptual dimensions, which represent overarch- ing categories encompassing related competencies. Multiple rounds of code reﬁnement and thematic vali- dation were conducted to ensure internal consistency and comprehensive representation of the data. The ﬁnal thematic structure was reviewed and validated by all authors.

The entire analysis was guided by our three research questions, which served as the organizing framework for interpreting the ﬁndings. This approach enabled a nuanced understanding of faculty AI literacy, captur- ing both ﬁne-grained competencies and broader conceptual constructs within this emerging ﬁeld.

# 3. Results

### _3.1. RQ1: how is faculty AI literacy deﬁned and conceptualized in the higher education literature?_

Of the 27 reviewed empirical studies, 20 of them explicitly deﬁned AI literacy or related concepts. Studies speciﬁcally addressing faculty AI literacy in higher education settings were relatively uncommon, even among those that clearly deﬁned it. The ﬁeld appears to be in its early stages of conceptual development, with researchers drawing from various theoretical frameworks to understand this emerging phenomenon.

8 Y. WU AND Y. HUANG

***3.1.1. Foundational frameworks and deﬁnitions*** Our review revealed that the majority of studies (12 out of 20) were built upon Ng et al.’s (2021b) founda- tional framework, which conceptualizes AI literacy as comprising four core dimensions: (a) understanding AI concepts, (b) applying AI in practical contexts, (c) critically evaluating AI technologies, and (d) comprehend- ing ethical implications. This framework has become particularly in uential in educational contexts, as evi- denced by its adoption in studies by Xie et al. (2025), Ning, Zhang, et al. (2025), and several others.

Long and Magerko’s deﬁnition was also frequently referenced, deﬁning AI literacy as “a set of competen- cies that enables individuals to critically evaluate AI technologies; communicate and collaborate e ectively with AI; and use AI as a tool online, at home, and in the workplace.” (Long & Magerko, 2020) This deﬁnition emphasizes the practical application and collaborative aspects of AI literacy, which resonated particularly well with studies examining faculty perceptions and usage patterns.

### _3.1.2. Three distinct conceptualization approaches_ Through our analysis, we identiﬁed three primary approaches to conceptualizing faculty AI literacy: 

1. _Technical–pedagogical integration approach_: Several studies (Ning, Zhang, et al., 2025; Shi, 2025; J. Zhang & Zhang, 2024) emphasized the integration of technical AI competencies with pedagogical knowledge. For instance, Shi (2025) deﬁned teacher generative AI competencies as “the knowledge, skills, and atti- tudes required for teachers to integrate generative AI in educational practice in pedagogically and ethi- cally sound ways.” This approach re ects the unique position of faculty who must not only understand AI technology but also e ectively integrate it into teaching and research practices.
2. _Critical–ethical approach_: Studies such as those by Martínez et al. (2025) and Picasso et al. (2024) placed stronger emphasis on critical thinking and ethical considerations. Martínez et al. (2025) speciﬁcally focused on “the ability to critically analyze, interpret, and evaluate data (including AI-produced and AI-used data)” within a data justice framework, highlighting the importance of addressing bias, fairness, and social implications in AI applications.

3\. _Comprehensive multidimensional approach:_ A third group of studies adopted broader, multidimensional frameworks that encompassed technical, pedagogical, ethical, and social aspects. These studies recog- nized AI literacy as a complex construct requiring multiple competency areas.

### _3.1.3. Contextual variations and cultural considerations_

Our review also revealed signiﬁcant variations in how AI literacy was conceptualized across di erent cultural and institutional contexts. Studies in Asian contexts (particularly China) tended to emphasize systematic skill development and institutional integration, while European studies placed greater emphasis on ethical con- siderations and critical evaluation. For example, Xue (2025)’s study in China focused on digital literacy devel- opment within professional learning communities, while Spanish studies by Martínez et al. (2025) emphasized critical thinking and social justice perspectives.

### _3.1.4. Emerging concepts and terminology_

The ﬁeld has also seen the emergence of specialized terminology. Several studies distinguished between general AI literacy and more speciﬁc concepts such as “generative AI competencies” (Shi, 2025), “digital AI competencies” (Ng et al., 2023), and “AI-induced emotions” (Xie et al., 2025). This proliferation of terms re ects the ﬁeld’s attempt to capture the nuanced and rapidly evolving nature of AI technologies and their educational applications.

### _3.1.5. Gaps and conceptual challenges_

Despite this conceptual diversity, our review identiﬁed several signiﬁcant gaps. First, unlike the teacher data literacy ﬁeld, which has established deﬁnitions speciﬁcally tailored to educational leaders’ roles and respon- sibilities, AI literacy deﬁnitions have largely been generic rather than role-speciﬁc. Faculty members have unique responsibilities that distinguish them from other user groups, including research responsibilities, aca- demic freedom considerations, and the need to model appropriate AI use for students.

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 9

Second, there appeared to be limited attention to the disciplinary variations in AI literacy needs. Faculty in STEM ﬁelds may require di erent AI competencies compared to those in the humanities or social sciences, yet most deﬁnitions provided were discipline-agnostic.

Third, the rapid evolution of AI technologies, particularly generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, has created a temporal challenge, where deﬁnitions struggle to remain current and relevant.

***3.1.6. Proposed synthesis deﬁnition*** Based on our comprehensive review and analysis of the 27 studies, we propose that faculty AI literacy in higher education be deﬁned as follows:

Faculty members’ knowledge, skills, dispositions, and practices that enable them to thoughtfully and responsibly integrate AI technologies into their academic work by (a) understanding AI capabilities and limit- ations within their disciplinary context, (b) e ectively applying AI tools in teaching, research, and service activities, (c) critically evaluating AI outputs and implications, (d) maintaining ethical standards and academic integrity, (e) fostering students’ AI literacy development, and (f) adapting to the evolving AI landscape through continuous learning and professional development.

This deﬁnition acknowledges that AI literacy for faculty encompasses both technical competencies and professional judgment, ethical reasoning, and pedagogical expertise. It recognizes the unique roles and responsibilities of faculty members in higher education while providing exibility for disciplinary and con- textual variations. Moreover, it emphasizes the dynamic nature of AI literacy, requiring ongoing develop- ment and adaptation as technologies and applications continue to evolve.

The inclusion of practices alongside knowledge, skills, and dispositions re ects our understanding that AI literacy is not merely theoretical but must be demonstrated through actual engagement with AI technol- ogies in authentic academic contexts. This behavioral component is essential for the full development and application of AI literacy in higher education settings.

### _3.2.3. Institutional type and educational level_

The reviewed studies predominantly focused on higher education institutions, with 22 studies (81.5%) exam- ining university or college contexts exclusively. However, there was notable diversity in higher education institutional types. Research universities were most commonly studied (n = 12), followed by comprehensive universities (n = 6) and specialized institutions such as polytechnics or teacher education colleges (n = 4). Five studies (18.5%) adopted cross-level approaches, examining AI literacy across multiple educational levels from K-12 through higher education, re ecting recognition that AI literacy development occurs across the educational continuum. Notably, three studies speciﬁcally focused on teacher education pro- grams, highlighting the critical role of preparing future educators for AI integration.

12 Y. WU AND Y. HUANG

### _3.2.4. Disciplinary focus_ The disciplinary distribution of studies reveals both breadth and concentration in certain areas. The largest category was cross-disciplinary studies (n = 15; 55.6%), which examined AI literacy across multiple academic ﬁelds simultaneously. This approach recognizes that AI technologies impact diverse disciplines and that AI literacy may manifest di erently depending on the academic domain. Language education, particularly English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teaching, emerged as a signiﬁcant focus area with four studies (14.8%), likely re ecting the particular relevance of generative AI tools for language instruction and assessment.

Teacher education represented another substantial focus, with three studies (11.1%), emphasizing the importance of preparing future educators for AI integration. Engineering education, educational technology, and medical education were each the focus of one study (3.7%), while several studies examined speciﬁc dis- ciplinary combinations. The predominance of cross-disciplinary studies suggests that researchers recognize AI literacy as a transversal competency that cuts across traditional academic boundaries, though certain ﬁelds have received more focused attention due to their particular relevance to AI applications.

### _3.2.5. Research methods_ The methodological approaches employed in the reviewed studies are considerably diverse. Quantitative methods were most prevalent (n = 12; 44.4%), typically employing survey research with various statistical analyses, including structural equation modeling, correlation analysis, and descriptive statistics. Literature and systematic reviews constituted the second largest category (n = 6; 22.2%), re ecting the ﬁeld’s need to synthesize emerging knowledge and develop theoretical frameworks.

Mixed-methods approaches were employed in four studies (14.8%), combining quantitative surveys with qualitative interviews or focus groups to provide a more comprehensive understanding of faculty AI literacy experiences. Qualitative methods were used in three studies (11.1%) and typically employed case study designs, interviews, or ethnographic approaches to explore AI literacy development in depth. Two investi- gations (7.4%) were theoretical or conceptual studies, focusing on framework development and conceptual analysis.

Notably, several studies employed sophisticated analytical techniques, including partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), conﬁrmatory factor analysis (CFA), and latent class analysis, indicat- ing methodological rigor in quantitative investigations. The prevalence of survey research re ects the ﬁeld’s emphasis on measuring AI literacy levels and identifying factors in uencing faculty adoption and compe- tency development.

### _3.2.6. Sample characteristics_

Sample sizes varied considerably across studies, ranging from small-scale qualitative investigations with 9 participants to large-scale surveys with over 600 respondents. The median sample size for quantitative studies was approximately 230 participants. Chinese studies tended to report larger sample sizes, with several exceeding 400 participants, while European and Middle Eastern studies typically employed smaller, more focused samples.

Most studies focused exclusively on faculty members or teachers, though some included mixed samples incorporating students, administrators, or other stakeholders. Several studies speciﬁcally targeted pre- service teachers, recognizing the importance of preparing future educators for AI integration. The samples’ geographic and cultural diversity provides valuable insights into how AI literacy manifests in di erent educational contexts and cultural settings.

### _3.2.7. Data collection methods_

Survey questionnaires were the predominant data collection method (n = 18; 66.7%), typically employing Likert-type scales ranging from 4-point to 7-point formats. Many studies utilized validated instruments or adapted existing scales to measure AI literacy constructs. Online administration was most common, likely in uenced by the COVID-19 pandemic and the digital nature of AI technologies.

Interviews, often semi-structured, were employed in six studies (22.2%) to explore faculty experiences, perceptions, and challenges related to AI integration. Literature analysis was used in six studies, focusing 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 13

on systematic or scoping reviews. Some studies employed innovative data collection approaches, including artifact analysis, critical co-discovery activities, and professional learning community documentation.

Several studies triangulated data sources, combining surveys with interviews, observations, or document analysis to enhance validity and provide a comprehensive understanding of AI literacy phenomena. The pre- dominance of self-report measures re ects both practical constraints and the emphasis on understanding faculty perceptions and self-assessed competencies.

***3.3. RQ3: indicators and dimensions of faculty AI literacy across di*** ***erent academic contexts, disciplines, and institutional settings***

Based on the systematic analysis of AI literacy indicators extracted from 27 studies, we identiﬁed six core dimensions comprising 39 speciﬁc indicators that consistently emerged across diverse academic contexts. These dimensions encompass both universal competencies for AI integration and contextual adaptations for speciﬁc educational environments. To transcend fragmented descriptions of tool-speciﬁc skills, this study synthesizes these indicators into six interconnected cognitive and practical dimensions. As illustrated in Figure 4, the framework is not a static linear list but a concentric structure centered on “future-adaptive professionalism.” This visualization captures the dynamic evolution of literacy development, transitioning from mere technical acquisition to profound value transformation.

The strength of the association between individual studies and each dimension is quantitatively rep- resented in [Figure 5,](#331-dimension-1-technical-understanding-and-application-the-ﬁrst-dimension-encompassed-nine-indicators-related-to-faculty-members-fundamental-ai-knowledge-and-practical-application-skills-as-detailed-in-table-a1) which presents a comprehensive heatmap analysis. Each cell in the matrix represents the relevance score (0–5 scale) of a particular study for a speciﬁc dimension, with the color gradient ranging from blue (no relevance, score 0) to red (highest relevance, score 5). This visualization enables identiﬁcation

of research gaps, areas of concentrated scholarly attention, and the relative emphasis placed on di erent aspects of faculty AI literacy across the reviewed literature.

The strength of the association between individual studies and each dimension is quantitatively rep- resented in [Figure 5,](#331-dimension-1-technical-understanding-and-application-the-ﬁrst-dimension-encompassed-nine-indicators-related-to-faculty-members-fundamental-ai-knowledge-and-practical-application-skills-as-detailed-in-table-a1) which provides a visualized topography of the current research landscape. The predo- minant deep-red clusters in Dimension 1 (Technical Understanding and Application) objectively indicate that the academic community remains in a tool-chasing stage, where empirical attention is heavily focused on the functional adoption of speciﬁc technologies. Conversely, the prevalence of cool-toned blue regions in Dimension 3 (Ethical Responsibility) serves as a cautionary signal; it highlights a signiﬁcant empirical deﬁcit in addressing social justice, algorithmic bias, and ethical risks during the rapid push for AI integration. Furthermore, the heterogeneous patterns observed in Dimension 5 and Dimension 6 suggest that while these areas are gaining recognition, they lack the systematic research focus necessary to move beyond anec- dotal accounts into robust, evidence-based pedagogical frameworks.

### _3.3.1. Dimension 1: technical understanding and application_ The ﬁrst dimension encompassed nine indicators related to faculty members’ fundamental AI knowledge and practical application skills, as detailed in [Table A1.](#appendix-a)

We found a comprehensive range of speciﬁc indicators in this dimension, including understanding fun- damental AI concepts, principles, and mechanisms (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#author-contributions) Ning, Zhang, et al., 2025; Zhang, Ganapathy Prasad, et al., 2025), identifying di erent types of AI tools and their functional characteristics (Hoang, 2025; Shi, 2025; Xie et al., 2025), mastering prompt engineering skills (Chen et al., [2024;](#author-contributions) Martínez et al., 2025; Seker et al., 2025), proﬁciently using various AI platforms (Khan et al., 2024; Wut et al., 2025; Xue, 2025), and e ectively aligning AI tools with teaching objectives (Lérias et al., 2024; Wang, Zhang, et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2024). This suggests that faculty members, as frontline educators and researchers, need to be involved in all aspects of AI-related technical knowledge and practical skills.

One might expect basic AI operation tasks to be handled by technical support sta , while faculty assume primarily instructional roles. However, we found that the AI literacy of faculty also includes speciﬁc hands-on technical competencies, such as debugging and optimizing AI tool outputs (Galindo-Domínguez et al., 2024; Mah & Groß, 2024) and mastering prompt engineering techniques (Chen et al., [2024;](#author-contributions) Shi, 2025; Wang, Zhang, et al., 2025), alongside their pedagogical responsibilities, such as designing AI-enhanced teaching activities and assessments (Alagöz Hamzaj, [2025;](#author-contributions) Dilek et al., [2025)](#author-contributions) and utilizing AI to support personalized instruction 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 15

(Chan & Tsi, [2024;](#author-contributions) Hoang, 2025). In other words, faculty were not limited to using pre-conﬁgured AI solutions; they were also active participants in the AI customization and optimization phases.

Faculty members also need to have a comprehensive understanding of AI capabilities and limitations in di erent contexts. For example, engineering faculty members require deeper technical knowledge, includ- ing AI model architectures and algorithmic bias sources (Zhang, Zhang, et al., 2025), while language edu- cation faculty members were found to focus more on AI’s language-processing capabilities and translation accuracy (Hoang, 2025; Xie et al., 2025). Furthermore, technically literate faculty members may need to anticipate and address challenges when implementing AI tools in diverse educational settings or adapting to rapidly evolving AI technologies (Chen et al., [2024;](#author-contributions) Martínez et al., 2025).

Overall, our ﬁndings for this dimension suggest that faculty AI literacy includes a wide range of technical knowledge and skills comparable to those required by any professional e ectively using AI technologies. Therefore, educators must develop a level of AI proﬁciency that enables them to conﬁdently integrate these tools into their academic practice. However, we identiﬁed three unique characteristics speciﬁc to higher education faculty. The ﬁrst is an understanding of the pedagogical a ordances of di erent AI tools, ensuring that technology selection aligns with educational objectives rather than being driven by technological novelty. The second is faculty members’ need to maintain critical awareness of AI limitations and potential risks in educational contexts, particularly regarding accuracy, bias, and appropriateness for student learning. The third is faculty members’ ability to adapt AI applications to diverse student populations and learning environments while maintaining educational e ectiveness. Frequently mentioned challenges for faculty members include rapid technological change, insu cient training opportunities, and the need to balance AI e ciency with authentic learning experiences (Alagöz Hamzaj, [2025;](#author-contributions) Ning, Zhang, et al., 2025). These challenges are likely to impact the e ectiveness of technically proﬁcient faculty in their endea- vor to meaningfully integrate AI into their teaching and research practices.

### _3.3.2. Dimension 2: critical evaluation_

The second dimension comprised six indicators related to faculty members’ abilities to critically assess AI outputs and identify potential risks and limitations. We identiﬁed diverse indicators in this dimension, includ- ing critically evaluating the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated content (Martínez et al., 2025; Sperling et al., 2024), identifying bias and errors in AI outputs (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#author-contributions) Picasso et al., 2024), comparing AI outputs with authoritative sources (Ning, Zhang, et al., 2025; Zhang, Ganapathy Prasad, et al., 2025), identify- ing potential risks and limitations of AI use (Chen et al., [2024;](#author-contributions) Xie et al., 2025), assessing AI’s impact on learn- ing processes (Alagöz Hamzaj, [2025;](#author-contributions) Mah & Groß, 2024), and preventing inappropriate use of AI (Galindo- Domínguez et al., 2024; Khan et al., 2024). This indicates that faculty members must develop sophisticated analytical capabilities to navigate the complex landscape of AI-mediated educational environments.

The critical evaluation dimension revealed signiﬁcant disciplinary variations in assessment priorities and approaches. For instance, medical and health education contexts emphasized indicators such as assessing AI diagnostic accuracy and evaluating AI recommendations in clinical settings (Sperling et al., 2024), while humanities contexts focused more on evaluating AI creativity, originality, and cultural sensitivity (Galindo- Domínguez et al., 2024). Research-intensive universities prioritized faculty members’ abilities to evaluate AI research validity and methodological rigor (Mah & Groß, 2024), whereas teaching-focused institutions emphasized the assessment of AI’s educational e ectiveness and its impact on student learning (J. Zhang & Zhang, 2024).

Faculty members also demonstrated varying approaches to establishing quality benchmarks for AI outputs depending on their disciplinary expertise and institutional context. Language education faculty developed speciﬁc competencies in assessing AI-generated language quality and translation accuracy (Xie et al., 2025), while cross-disciplinary faculty focused on more general indicators such as systematic AI output validation and error detection capabilities (Ning, Zhang, et al., 2025). Furthermore, critical evaluation skills were closely linked to faculty members’ understanding of their professional responsibilities, with many recognizing the need to maintain human agency and professional judgment in AI-mediated decision- making processes (Martínez et al., 2025).

Our analysis revealed that e ective critical evaluation requires faculty members to develop meta-cogni- tive awareness about their own assessment processes and potential blind spots when working with AI systems. This dimension proved particularly challenging for faculty members who were enthusiastic early 

16 Y. WU AND Y. HUANG

adopters of AI technologies, as they sometimes struggled to maintain appropriate skepticism about AI capa- bilities while exploring innovative applications (Chen et al., [2024)](#author-contributions). The critical evaluation dimension thus rep- resents a crucial checkpoint that prevents both over-reliance on AI systems and premature dismissal of potentially valuable AI applications in educational contexts.

### _3.3.3. Dimension 3: ethical responsibility_ The third dimension consisted of six indicators addressing faculty members’ understanding and implemen- tation of ethical principles in AI use. This dimension encompassed following ethical principles and guidelines for AI use (Martínez et al., 2025; Ning, Zhang, et al., 2025; Picasso et al., 2024), understanding fairness and transparency requirements in AI applications (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#author-contributions) Sperling et al., 2024), ensuring AI use com- plies with academic integrity standards (Chen et al., [2024;](#author-contributions) Shi, 2025), protecting student data privacy and security (Alagöz Hamzaj, [2025;](#author-contributions) Chan & Tsi, [2024)](#author-contributions), understanding data protection regulatory requirements (Khan et al., 2024; Martínez et al., 2025), and establishing transparency protocols for AI use (Hoang, 2025; Wut et al., 2025). This comprehensive ethical framework re ects the complex moral landscape that faculty members must navigate when integrating AI technologies into their professional practice.

The ethical responsibility dimension showed remarkable consistency across di erent cultural and insti- tutional contexts, suggesting universal recognition of fundamental ethical principles in AI use. However, the speciﬁc manifestations and emphases of ethical concerns varied signiﬁcantly. European studies particu- larly emphasized maintaining human agency in AI-mediated environments and preserving democratic values (Martínez et al., 2025), re ecting regional regulatory frameworks and cultural values, while Chinese studies focused more on institutional responsibility and collective ethical standards (Ning, Zhang, et al., 2025), and Middle Eastern research emphasized cultural appropriateness and value alignment (Al-Abdullatif, [2024)](#author-contributions).

Faculty ethical responsibility extended beyond individual decision-making to encompass broader pro- fessional and social obligations. Teacher education contexts revealed unique ethical indicators, including modeling responsible AI use for future educators and ensuring developmental appropriateness in AI appli- cations (Alagöz Hamzaj, [2025)](#author-contributions). Research contexts emphasized understanding AI’s impact on research integ- rity and transparent reporting of AI assistance (Chen et al., [2024)](#author-contributions). Data justice perspectives highlighted the importance of understanding AI’s impact on marginalized communities and advocating for equitable acces- s(Picasso et al., 2024).

The ethical dimension also revealed tension between innovation and responsibility, as faculty members sought to explore AI’s educational potential while maintaining ethical safeguards. Many studies indicated that faculty members struggled with balancing transparency about AI use with concerns about student anxiety or resistance (Chan & Tsi, [2024)](#author-contributions). Additionally, institutional variations in ethical guidelines and support systems signiﬁcantly in uenced faculty’s ability to implement consistent ethical practices (Khan et al., 2024). This dimension thus represents not only individual moral competency but also collective pro- fessional responsibility for shaping ethical AI integration in higher education.

### _3.3.4. Dimension 4: teaching innovation_

The fourth dimension included six indicators related to faculty members’ abilities to creatively integrate AI technologies into their teaching practice and develop innovative pedagogical approaches. Key indicators encompassed using AI to create personalized learning experiences, designing AI-assisted interactive teach- ing activities (Dilek et al., [2025;](#author-contributions) Xia et al., 2024), developing AI-enhanced assessment methods (Hoang, 2025; Wang, Zhang, et al., 2025), exploring AI-supported new teaching models (Mah & Groß, 2024; Seker et al., 2025), using AI to promote collaborative learning (Chen et al., [2024;](#author-contributions) Galindo-Domínguez et al., 2024), and providing immediate feedback through AI (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#author-contributions) Xie et al., 2025). This dimension represents the creative and transformative potential of AI integration in higher education.

The teaching innovation dimension demonstrated signiﬁcant variation across disciplinary contexts and institutional types. Language education was particularly rich in innovation indicators, including AI-assisted language assessment, personalized vocabulary instruction, and culturally responsive language-learning experiences (Hoang, 2025; Xie et al., 2025). Engineering education emphasized AI applications in project- based learning, simulation-enhanced instruction, and collaborative problem-solving environments (Zhang, 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 17

Zhang, et al., 2025). Teacher education contexts revealed unique innovation focuses, including preparing future educators to integrate AI and modeling innovative pedagogical practices (Shi, 2025).

The institutional setting signiﬁcantly in uenced the scope and nature of teaching innovations possible with AI integration. Research universities emphasized sophisticated applications such as AI-enhanced research methodology instruction and graduate student mentoring support (Seker et al., 2025), while teach- ing-focused institutions prioritized undergraduate learning enhancement and student engagement strat- egies (Lérias et al., 2024). Private institutions showed greater exibility in experimenting with cutting- edge AI applications, while public institutions focused more on scalable and cost-e ective implementations (Wut et al., 2025).

Faculty members’ innovation capabilities were closely linked to their technical proﬁciency and insti- tutional support systems. Successful innovators demonstrated the ability to envision pedagogical possibili- ties that extended beyond simple task automation to fundamental transformation of learning experiences (Xue, 2025). However, innovation e orts were often constrained by institutional policies, student readiness, and resource limitations (Dilek et al., [2025)](#author-contributions). The teaching innovation dimension thus represents both indi- vidual creativity and the systemic capacity for educational transformation through AI integration.

### _3.3.5. Dimension 5: professional development_

The ﬁfth dimension comprised six indicators addressing faculty members’ commitment to continuous learn- ing and professional growth in AI literacy. This dimension included keeping up with the latest developments in AI technology (Ning, Zhang, et al., 2025; Seker et al., 2025; Zhang, Ganapathy Prasad, et al., 2025), parti- cipating in AI-education-related professional development activities (Alagöz Hamzaj, [2025;](#author-contributions) Dilek et al., [2025;](#author-contributions) Shi, 2025), building professional learning networks for AI education (Hoang, 2025; Xue, 2025), sharing AI teaching experiences and best practices with colleagues (Khan et al., 2024; Mah & Groß, 2024; Wut et al., 2025), mentoring other faculty members in AI tool integration (Chen et al., [2024;](#author-contributions) Galindo-Domínguez et al., 2024), and participating in AI education policy and practice discussions (Martínez et al., 2025; Picasso et al., 2024). This dimension re ects the dynamic and collaborative nature of AI literacy development in aca- demic contexts.

The professional development dimension revealed signiﬁcant variation in learning approaches and pre- ferences across di erent faculty populations. Experienced faculty members often preferred informal learning through peer networks and collaborative experimentation (Xue, 2025), while newer faculty members showed greater interest in structured training programs and formal professional development opportunities (Alagöz Hamzaj, [2025)](#author-contributions). Disciplinary di erences were also evident, with technical ﬁelds emphasizing hands- on workshops and tool-speciﬁc training, while humanities ﬁelds focused more on conceptual understanding and ethical implications (Galindo-Domínguez et al., 2024).

The institutional context signiﬁcantly in uenced professional development opportunities and expec- tations. Research universities provided more resources for faculty to attend conferences and participate in AI research collaborations (Seker et al., 2025), while teaching-focused institutions emphasized practical skill development and classroom application training (Dilek et al., [2025)](#author-contributions). International contexts revealed additional complexity, with faculty members in developing countries facing greater challenges in accessing current AI education resources and professional development opportunities (Chen et al., [2024)](#author-contributions).

The collaborative aspect of this dimension proved particularly important for sustaining AI literacy devel- opment over time. Faculty members who engaged in professional learning communities and peer mentor- ing relationships demonstrated more sustained and sophisticated AI integration practices (Xue, 2025).

Similar insights can be drawn from the ﬁeld of entrepreneurship education, where structured experiential interventions such as competitions have been shown to e ectively mediate the relationship between edu- cational policy and competence development (Li et al., 2023). This suggests that AI literacy development could similarly beneﬁt from institutionally supported, practice-oriented activities, such as AI-enhanced teaching contests, hackathons, or cross-disciplinary learning hubs, that foster authentic engagement and competence construction.

Leadership roles in AI education initiatives provided additional professional development opportunities while contributing to institutional capacity-building (Hoang, 2025). This dimension thus represents both individual commitment to lifelong learning and collective responsibility for advancing AI literacy across the academic profession.

This dimension represents faculty’s forward-looking responsi- bility for student success in an AI-integrated society.

The student development dimension showed strong alignment with broader educational goals while adapting to AI-speciﬁc competencies and challenges. Faculty members recognized the need to balance AI skill development with critical thinking and ethical awareness, ensuring that students become sophisticated AI users rather than passive consumers of AI-generated content (Martínez et al., 2025). This balance proved particularly challenging in disciplines where AI tools could potentially replace traditional skill development, requiring faculty to reimagine learning objectives and assessment practices (Xie et al., 2025).

Disciplinary contexts signiﬁcantly in uenced approaches to student AI literacy development. Teacher education programs emphasized preparing future educators to integrate AI responsibly in their own teach- ing practice (Alagöz Hamzaj, [2025)](#author-contributions), while language education focused on maintaining authentic communi- cation skills in AI-mediated environments (Hoang, 2025). Professional programs in business and engineering emphasized workplace readiness and human–AI collaboration skills (Lérias et al., 2024; J. Zhang & Zhang, 2024).

Faculty members’ approaches to student development revealed varying philosophies about AI’s role in education and society. Some faculty members emphasized AI as a tool for enhancing human capabilities and creativity (Dilek et al., [2025)](#author-contributions), while others focused more on critical evaluation and resistance to over- dependence on AI systems (Sperling et al., 2024). Cultural contexts also in uenced student development pri- orities, with some emphasizing collective responsibility and social impact (Ning, Zhang, et al., 2025) and others focusing more on individual skills and career preparation (Chan & Tsi, [2024)](#author-contributions). This dimension thus rep- resents faculty’s role as bridges between current educational practice and future societal needs in an AI-inte- grated world.

These six dimensions collectively describe how faculty AI literacy operates as a complex system in uen- cing decision-making, teaching, and institutional innovation. A comprehensive list of corresponding indi- cators is included in Appendix 1 ([Table A1)](#appendix-a). To enhance the theoretical coherence of our synthesized framework, we examined its alignment with established conceptual models, as illustrated in [Table 4.](#336-dimension-6-student-development-support) This comparative analysis demonstrates how our six identiﬁed dimensions can be meaningfully mapped onto the four-aspect AI literacy framework widely recognized in the educational technology literature (Ng et al., 2021b). For example, AI conceptual understanding and technical proﬁciency correspond closely to the “Know and Understand AI” and “Apply AI” aspects, respectively. Ethical and responsible AI use aligns closely with the “AI Ethics” aspect, while instructional innovation and student development support jointly re ect the evaluative and creative competencies emphasized in the “Evaluate and Create AI” domain. Additionally, Ongoing professional learning, although not explicitly included in the original four- aspect model, expands on the notion of continuous engagement with AI by addressing faculty members’ evolving professional identity and institutional responsibilities. # 4. Discussion

The primary aims of this review were (a) to clarify what constitutes faculty AI literacy in higher education, including its deﬁnitions, indicators, and dimensions, and (b) to examine how faculty AI literacy di ers from that of educational professionals in general. Across 27 empirical studies, we identiﬁed 39 indicators across six dimensions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst systematic synthesis of faculty AI literacy research within higher education, providing a foundational framework for this rapidly emerging ﬁeld.

## _4.1. Comprehensive understanding of faculty AI literacy_

This section conceptualizes faculty AI literacy as a systemic pillar of future-adaptive professionalism. By dis- tilling 39 indicators into six core dimensions, the framework distinguishes faculty-speciﬁc competencies from generic digital literacy, anchoring them within the core domains of academic work – discovery, pedagogy, and leadership. This reframing positions AI literacy not as a transient technical skill but as an enduring com- ponent of digital academic identity.

### _4.1.1. Core dimensions and conceptual features_

Our proposed deﬁnition of faculty AI literacy has four distinct features. First, it acknowledges the multiple ways faculty members engage with AI across their professional responsibilities, captured by the six dimen- sions: Dimension 1 (Technical Understanding and Application), Dimension 2 (Critical Evaluation), Dimension 3 (Ethical Responsibility), Dimension 4 (Teaching Innovation), Dimension 5 (Professional Development), and Dimension 6 (Student Development Support).

Second, whereas traditional deﬁnitions of AI literacy primarily emphasize technical knowledge, such as “understanding AI concepts, applying AI in practical contexts, and using AI as a tool” (Long & Magerko, 2020; Ng et al., 2021b), our analysis reveals that faculty AI literacy extends well beyond these competencies. Faculty must also critically assess AI appropriateness, maintain ethical standards, innovate pedagogical prac- tices, and guide institutional AI integration. This broader scope re ects the dual role of faculty as both users and leaders of educational technology.

Third, our deﬁnition foregrounds dispositions and attitudes. The reviewed studies consistently empha- sized that successful AI literacy requires not only knowledge and skills but also appropriate mindsets toward AI acceptance, ethics, and continuous learning (Alagöz Hamzaj, [2025;](#author-contributions) Galindo-Domínguez et al., 2024; Wut et al., 2025). Dispositions are crucial because they (a) translate abstract competencies into action- able outcomes in teaching and research, (b) create a foundation for ongoing professional growth in a rapidly evolving technological landscape, and (c) sustain meaningful AI integration rather than superﬁcial adoption.

Finally, our deﬁnition is context-speciﬁc to higher education. While previous researchers have often bor- rowed deﬁnitions from K-12 or general populations (e.g. Chen et al., [2024;](#author-contributions) Martínez et al., 2025; Seker et al., 2025). While previous researchers have often borrowed deﬁnitions from K-12 or general populations (e.g. Al- Abdullatif, [2024;](#author-contributions) Ning, Zhang, et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025), these do not fully capture the demands placed on university faculty, including advanced research methodologies, graduate-level pedagogy, scholarly com- munication, interdisciplinary collaboration, and institutional leadership. Faculty serve as knowledge creators and institutional leaders, requiring a level of AI literacy that integrates critical thinking with the capacity to drive institutional transformation.

### _4.1.2. Theoretical reframing: situating the framework within Boyer’s scholarship model_

To strengthen the framework’s theoretical foundations, we map the six dimensions onto Boyer’s ([1990)](#author-contributions) scho- larship model, encompassing discovery, teaching, integration, and application. This mapping shifts the focus from discrete technical skills toward a holistic understanding of digital academic professionalism, revealing how AI fundamentally reshapes the core practices of scholarly work.

_The scholarship of discovery: from individual heroism to socio-technical collaboration_. In knowledge cre- ation, Dimensions 1 (Technical Understanding) and 2 (Critical Evaluation) re ect a fundamental shift in 

20 Y. WU AND Y. HUANG

knowledge creation. AI now functions as an active co-researcher that redeﬁnes what constitutes academic evidence. This requires faculty to move from traditional individual inquiry toward collaboration within socio- technical systems, exercising agency to ensure that algorithmic logic does not eclipse scholarly rigor.

_The scholarship of teaching: reclaiming agency in algorithmic mediation_. In AI-enhanced learning environ- ments, AI serves as a co-mentor (Cribb & Gewirtz, [2025)](#author-contributions), reconﬁguring the relationship between educators and students. Embodied in Dimensions 4 (Teaching Innovation) and 6 (Student Development Support), this scholarship demands a shift from content delivery to the strategic navigation of algorithmic mediation. Faculty agency ensures that human-centered relational pedagogy remains central to knowledge construc- tion within the student-instructor-AI interface. Teaching scholarship is thus redeﬁned as the capacity to guide students through critical collaboration with intelligent systems.

_The scholarship of integration and application: systemic governance and collective stewardship_. Aligned with Dimensions 3 (Ethical Responsibility) and 5 (Professional Development), AI literacy functions as a distributed collective capability rather than an isolated individual attribute. Drawing on Activity Theory, faculty demon- strate academic professionalism through ethical stewardship within the university’s socio-technical architec- ture, serving as _educational value leaders_ who navigate the shifting socio-technical imaginaries (Jasano , 2015) of the AI era. This positions faculty not merely as tool users but as guardians of the academic commu- nity’s collective intelligence.

## _4.2. Unique characteristics and future-adaptive mechanisms of faculty AI literacy_

Faculty AI literacy is distinguished not only by the complexity of academic roles but also by mechanisms that ensure its long-term relevance. We categorize these into role-speciﬁc distinctiveness and principle-based adaptive mechanisms.

#### _4.2.1. Role-speciﬁc distinctiveness in the higher education ecosystem_

Unlike general educator competencies, faculty AI literacy is deeply intertwined with the tripartite academic roles of research, teaching, and service. First, _Research Integration Complexity_ requires faculty to navigate AI- assisted methodologies and literature synthesis while maintaining data integrity (Ekundayo et al., 2024; Perkins & Roe, 2024). Second, _Graduate-Level Pedagogical Sophistication_ demands that faculty mentor emer- ging scholars in AI-enhanced environments, balancing tool e ciency with the development of students’ original scholarly voices.

Third, _Disciplinary Expertise Integration_ ensures that AI tools align with speciﬁc disciplinary epistemologies, for example, algorithmic rigor in medical sciences (Sperling et al., 2024) versus maintaining human agency in humanities-based inquiries (Martínez et al., 2025). Fourth, _Institutional Leadership and Policy In_ _uence_ pos- itions faculty as active agents in academic governance, shaping AI policies at the university level (Hoang, 2025). Together, these roles demand a specialized literacy that extends beyond functional tool usage to encompass high-level professional judgment.

### _4.2.2. Operationalizing adaptability: the multi-layered dynamics of the framework_

To address the rapid obsolescence of tool-speciﬁc models, this framework operates as a dynamic system rather than a static taxonomy. Its adaptability is realized through four hierarchical levels:

_Level 4: the empirical foundation_. The six operational dimensions provide indicators for navigating current AI systems. These act as updatable sensors that can be reconﬁgured as new tools emerge without destabiliz- ing the overall framework.

_Level 3: meta-competency drive_. This is the core mechanism for future-readiness. By prioritizing algorithmic logic, critical reasoning, and interdisciplinary linkage, the framework o ers an anchor that transcends speciﬁc platforms. These meta-competencies safeguard digital agency, preventing faculty from being alienated, a process where scholarly judgment is progressively substituted by automated logic. This resilience is particu- larly vital in resource-constrained academic environments, where the tension between technological _promise and precarity_ is most acute (Hamamra et al., 2025). In such contexts, meta-competencies act as a critical bu er, enabling faculty to maintain pedagogical leadership even when institutional supports are unstable.

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 21

_Level 2: theoretical pillars_. Anchoring AI literacy within Boyer’s scholarship model provides a stable pro- fessional context: as long as the university’s core missions of discovery and teaching endure, the framework remains relevant.

_Level 1: the target state_. The ﬁnal state is not a ﬁxed destination but a process of “Future-Adaptive Profes- sionalism,” actualized through continuous re ective cycles and active adaptation. AI integration thus becomes an evolving scholarly practice rather than a one-time skill acquisition.

To further clarify the distinction between stable and evolving components, [Table 5](#43-applicability-across-higher-education-contexts) categorizes the frame- work’s elements by their expected temporal stability.

This distinction illustrates how the framework absorbs technological change. When a new AI paradigm emerges, such as the shift from current LLMs to autonomous AI agents, Level 4 indicators (e.g. speciﬁc tool proﬁciency) would require updating, while Level 3 meta-competencies (e.g. critical evaluation of algo- rithmic decision-making) and Level 2 theoretical pillars remain stable. For instance, autonomous AI systems in research would demand new operational skills (e.g. supervising AI-driven experimental designs), but the underlying meta-competency of maintaining human agency in knowledge creation would persist and become even more critical.

It should be emphasized that the reference to autonomous AI systems is intended to be illustrative rather than predictive, serving to demonstrate how the proposed framework accommodates emerging technologi- cal paradigms, rather than to forecast speciﬁc trajectories of AI development.

## _4.3. Applicability across higher education contexts_

Faculty AI literacy is not monolithic; its application is heavily mediated by disciplinary and institutional con- texts. This section elaborates on how the six dimensions are interpreted across heterogeneous academic environments.

#### _4.3.1. Disciplinary epistemologies and the reconﬁguration of AI literacy priorities_

While the core dimensions of the framework remain constant across disciplines, their relative emphasis varies according to disciplinary epistemologies and methodological traditions.

_STEM and medical sciences: algorithmic rigor and the veracity of evidence_. In positivist, empirically driven ﬁelds, AI literacy centers on the intersection of Dimensions 1 (Technical Understanding) and 2 (Critical Evalu- ation). Faculty must be able to interrogate AI black boxes to ensure the reliability of evidence claims. For medical educators, this means critically assessing algorithmic logic behind AI-generated diagnostic sugges- tions to safeguard clinical validity. In engineering, the priority lies in maintaining experimental reproducibil- ity amidst increasingly opaque AI-assisted simulations.

_Humanities and the arts: maintaining human agency and critiquing cultural bias_. In ﬁelds where knowledge is generated through interpretation, AI poses the risk of diluting the original scholarly voice. Here, Dimen- sions 3 (Ethical Responsibility) and 2 (Critical Evaluation) take precedence. Faculty literacy is demonstrated
